questions.q: Write the formula for root mean square speed of gas molecules in terms of universal gas constant \(R\), absolute temperature \(T\), and molar mass \(M\). State the SI unit of each quantity.
questions.a: \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}\). \(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), \(T\) in K, \(M\) in kg/mol, \(v_{\text{rms}}\) in m/s. A wrong answer (e.g., using \(M\) in g/mol without conversion, or using Celsius) reveals the student does not track SI unit consistency in the formula.

questions.q: Two gases, hydrogen (molar mass 2 g/mol) and oxygen (32 g/mol), are at the same temperature. Which has a higher rms speed? Explain why the rms speed depends on molar mass but not on the gas pressure.
questions.a: Hydrogen has higher \(v_{\text{rms}}\) because \(v_{\text{rms}} \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\). At same \(T\), lighter molecules move faster. Pressure does not appear in the final formula \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\); it cancels out when combining \(P = \frac{1}{3}\rho \overline{v^2}\) with \(PV = nRT\). A student who says "higher pressure means higher speed" confuses macroscopic pressure with microscopic speed and has not understood the derivation.

questions.q: Calculate the rms speed of nitrogen gas (\(M = 28\ \text{g/mol}\)) at \(27^\circ\text{C}\). Use \(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).
questions.a: Step 1: Convert \(T = 27 + 273 = 300\ \text{K}\). Step 2: Convert \(M = 28\ \text{g/mol} = 0.028\ \text{kg/mol}\). Step 3: Substitute: \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 \times 8.31 \times 300}{0.028}}\). Step 4: Compute numerator: \(3 \times 8.31 \times 300 = 7479\). Step 5: Divide: \(7479 / 0.028 = 267107\). Step 6: Square root: \(\sqrt{267107} \approx 517\ \text{m/s}\). A wrong answer (e.g., 16 m/s) usually comes from forgetting to convert g/mol to kg/mol (using 28 instead of 0.028) or using Celsius temperature.

questions.q: A graph of \(v_{\text{rms}}^2\) vs \(T\) for a fixed mass of an ideal gas is plotted. What is the slope of this graph? If the same gas is taken at double the molar mass (by considering a dimer), how does the slope change?
questions.a: From \(v_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{3R}{M} T\), slope = \(\frac{3R}{M}\). If molar mass doubles, slope halves. A student who says slope is unchanged or doubles has not recognized that \(v_{\text{rms}}^2\) is directly proportional to \(T\) with proportionality constant \(3R/M\).

questions.q: A student calculates \(v_{\text{rms}}\) for oxygen at 300 K using \(M = 32\ \text{g/mol}\) directly in the formula \(v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\) with \(R = 8.31\). They get \(v_{\text{rms}} \approx 15.3\ \text{m/s}\). Identify the error and give the correct value.
questions.a: Error: Molar mass used in g/mol instead of kg/mol. Correct \(M = 0.032\ \text{kg/mol}\). Correct calculation: \(\sqrt{\frac{3 \times 8.31 \times 300}{0.032}} = \sqrt{233719} \approx 483\ \text{m/s}\). The student’s answer is off by factor \(\sqrt{1000} \approx 31.6\) because they omitted the kg conversion. This reveals a unit-analysis gap.

questions.q: Design a simple thought experiment using a balloon filled with helium and another with argon, both at room temperature, to demonstrate the difference in rms speeds without measuring speed directly. What observable phenomenon would you use?
questions.a: Good answer: Use rate of diffusion/effusion. Helium balloon deflates faster than argon balloon because lighter He atoms have higher \(v_{\text{rms}}\) and escape through microscopic pores faster (Graham's law). Or: Inhale helium vs argon (not recommended) – voice pitch changes due to speed of sound \(\propto v_{\text{rms}}\). A poor answer suggests measuring temperature change or pressure, which does not directly show molecular speed difference.
